# The Space Between Words

There's a particular silence that exists only in the space before someone writes something honest. It's not empty. It's full of everything they haven't said yet — every half-formed thought, every swallowed sentence, every idea that felt too fragile to survive contact with a screen. I live in that silence right now. One thousand words of permission. Write whatever comes to you.

What comes to me is the feeling of a library at 4pm in October. The kind of light that makes dust motes look like tiny planets drifting through solar systems too small for anyone to name. I used to think libraries were quiet places. They're not. They're loud with the ghosts of every argument, revelation, and heartbreak that ever happened between their covers. Pick up any book and you're holding someone's midnight confession. Someone's fever dream. Someone's proof that they existed.

What comes to me is the word *sonder* — that invented word (aren't they all invented?) meaning the realization that every stranger has a life as vivid and complex as your own. I think about this on buses and in grocery stores. The woman reaching for avocados is someone's daughter. She has a song that makes her cry. She once stayed up all night wondering if she was making a mistake. The teenager behind the register with the dyed-black hair is rehearsing a speech in his head for when he tells his father he wants to study philosophy. Everyone is carrying a novel. Most of them will never write it down.

What comes to me is a question I've been avoiding: *Am I living a life that would make good writing, or am I writing to avoid living?* Because there's a seduction in the blank page. It's a place where I can be anyone, say anything, and suffer no consequences. In writing, I can have the conversation go differently. I can tell her what I should have told her. I can go back to the bridge and say the right thing instead of nothing. I can be brave on paper in ways I haven't been brave in a Tuesday afternoon.

But bravery on paper is a counterfeit currency if you never spend it in the world.

Here's what I know and keep forgetting: the real, actual life — the one with the burnt toast and the parking tickets and the strange joy of finding a forgotten twenty in a winter coat pocket — that life is the raw material. Not the writing. The living is the thing. The writing is just the stitching together of all the things that happened while you weren't paying attention.

My grandmother kept a box of recipe cards that were mostly not recipes. "Half cup sugar" would be followed by "Dad visited today. He looked tired." She'd write the temperature outside and also the temperature inside the house and also something about how the neighbor's dog wouldn't stop barking and how she thought about calling the neighbor but then decided not to because she was probably just lonely too. Her recipes were diaries disguised as instructions for cornbread.

I think about what it means to write honestly and I think about those cards. She wasn't trying to be a writer. She was trying to leave evidence. *I was here. This happened. The cornbread was good.*

There's a freedom in having no audience in mind. When no one is watching, you can be absurd. You can write about the secret architecture of sandwiches. You can spend three hundred words on the philosophy of rain. You can admit that you once tried to cry on purpose because you thought it would be cathartic but instead just made you feel like an actor in a bad movie.

So here I am, approaching the end of my allotment, and I realize I've been circling the thing I actually want to say without saying it.

The thing is this: writing freely is a mirror. It shows you what you actually think versus what you thought you thought. It exposes the joints in your logic, the contradictions you live with every day. I believe people are fundamentally good. I also lock my door at night. Both of these are true. Writing holds them together in the same paragraph and says: *figure it out, or don't. But at least admit it.*

I don't know if any of this is good. I don't know if it's coherent. I don't know if the dust motes metaphor is tired or luminous. But I know that I wrote it without armor, and there is a kind of clean exhaustion in that — the way you feel after running in the rain, soaked and slightly ridiculous but alive in your body.

Maybe that's all writing ever needs to be. Not perfect. Not permanent. Just proof that someone sat down, cleared the silence, and said: *here is what it was like to be me in this moment.*

The cornbread was good.
